title: 1 Samuel 3:1–10
context: In a time when the LORD’s word was rare, the boy Samuel, serving under the aging Eli at the sanctuary, hears the LORD call his name three times and runs to Eli each time, until Eli realizes the LORD is calling and teaches him to answer. When the LORD calls again, Samuel replies, “Speak; for your servant hears.” Both traditions read this as shared ground on God’s gracious initiative in calling and the fitting response of attentive obedience.

verses.text: The child Samuel ministered to the LORD before Eli. The LORD’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions, then.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samuel ministers before the LORD under Eli, in days when the LORD’s word was rare and visions were few. Arminian readers note that the scarcity of revelation fits the spiritual decline described in chapter 2.

Silence from God is treated as a sign of trouble in Israel (cf. Amos 8:11), which makes the coming call all the more striking.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s sovereign freedom in when and to whom he speaks. The rarity of the word sets the stage for God to raise up a new prophet.

The boy’s faithful service in an unfaithful time shows God preserving a remnant before he speaks again.

verses.text: At that time, when Eli was laid down in his place (now his eyes had begun to grow dim, so that he could not see),
verses.arminianNotes:
Eli lies in his place, his eyes growing dim so that he could not see. Arminian readers note that the physical detail may also echo Eli’s failing spiritual perception, though the text states only his eyesight.

The narrator carefully sets the night scene before the call.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the contrast between the aging priest and the boy who will hear God’s voice.

The detail of Eli’s dim eyes prepares for his reliance on Samuel and for later scenes (4:15). Any symbolic sense is a reading, not a statement of the text.

verses.text: and God’s lamp hadn’t yet gone out, and Samuel had laid down in the LORD’s temple where God’s ark was,
verses.arminianNotes:
God’s lamp had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying in the LORD’s temple where the ark was. Arminian readers note that the lamp burned through the night (cf. Exod 27:20–21), so the scene is set before dawn.

Many readers also hear a hint that Israel’s light, though dim, had not yet been extinguished.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s presence still among his people, symbolized by the ark, even in a dark period.

The phrase about the lamp is a time marker and, for many readers, a quiet sign of hope. The call comes near the ark, the place of God’s throne.

verses.text: The LORD called Samuel. He said, “Here I am.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD calls Samuel, and he answers, “Here I am.” Arminian readers note the boy’s ready response, even though he does not yet recognize the voice.

God’s call comes personally, by name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the call begins with God. Samuel does not seek this encounter; the LORD initiates it.

The answer “Here I am” echoes the responses of Abraham and Moses (Gen 22:1; Exod 3:4).

verses.text: He ran to Eli and said, “Here I am; for you called me.” He said, “I didn’t call. Lie down again.” He went and lay down.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samuel runs to Eli, thinking Eli called, and Eli sends him back to bed. Arminian readers note Samuel’s eagerness and the gentle humor of the misunderstanding.

Genuine readiness to serve is present even before understanding.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the boy’s obedience to his human master as a preparation for obedience to God.

The repeated misunderstanding shows that recognizing God’s voice is not automatic; it must be learned and given.

verses.text: The LORD called yet again, “Samuel!” Samuel arose and went to Eli and said, “Here I am; for you called me.” He answered, “I didn’t call, my son. Lie down again.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD calls again, and again Samuel goes to Eli, who says, “I didn’t call, my son. Lie down again.” Arminian readers note God’s patience in repeating the call.

God does not abandon the call when it is not immediately understood.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see God’s persistence in calling. The repetition shows that the call will not fail.

Eli’s tender “my son” contrasts with his failure toward his own sons in chapter 2.

verses.text: Now Samuel didn’t yet know the LORD, neither was the LORD’s word yet revealed to him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the LORD’s word had not yet been revealed to him. Arminian readers read this not as unbelief but as the absence of direct revelation so far.

Samuel served faithfully before he received prophetic knowledge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also understand the verse as describing the lack of personal revelation, not hostility to God.

Knowing the LORD in this sense comes through his word revealed. Both traditions read the verse as an explanation of Samuel’s confusion.

verses.text: The LORD called Samuel again the third time. He arose and went to Eli and said, “Here I am; for you called me.” Eli perceived that the LORD had called the child.
verses.arminianNotes:
After the third call, Eli perceives that the LORD is calling the boy. Arminian readers note that Eli, despite his failures, helps Samuel respond rightly.

God can use flawed leaders to guide others.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God working through Eli’s insight. The aging priest recognizes what is happening.

The third call brings understanding; God’s purpose moves forward despite human slowness.

verses.text: Therefore Eli said to Samuel, “Go, lie down. It shall be, if he calls you, that you shall say, ‘Speak, LORD; for your servant hears.’ ” So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eli tells Samuel to answer, “Speak, LORD; for your servant hears.” Arminian readers note the importance of spiritual mentoring in learning to respond to God.

The words model humble readiness to listen and obey.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the value of instruction. Eli teaches the right posture before God’s word.

The response joins listening and servanthood, a pattern for all who hear God’s word.

verses.text: The LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, “Samuel! Samuel!” Then Samuel said, “Speak; for your servant hears.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD comes, stands, and calls, “Samuel! Samuel!” and Samuel answers, “Speak; for your servant hears.” Arminian readers note the double call, like those to Abraham and Moses (Gen 22:11; Exod 3:4).

Samuel responds willingly to God’s personal call.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s personal presence in the call. The LORD “came, and stood.”

Samuel’s answer leaves out the word “LORD” that Eli suggested, a detail interpreters note without agreeing on its meaning.
